title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

report.summary: A new benchmark finds nine frontier AI agents can draft scientific follow-up papers, but none satisfy domain experts, with most failing integrity checks.
report.background: AI agents are increasingly proposed as tools for scientific discovery, but most benchmarks test closed tasks with known answers. Open research problems lack reference solutions, making evaluation difficult. To address this, researchers worked with scientists at US Department of Energy national laboratories, who contributed unpublished follow-up directions from their own work and listed conditions a valid submission must meet. These conditions become a rubric for judging papers on problems with no ground truth. The benchmark spans quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning, testing whether agents can generate publishable follow-ups. It reflects growing interest in autonomous research agents and concerns about evaluation, reproducibility, and scientific integrity.
key_points: The benchmark gives an AI agent a published science paper plus an unpublished follow-up direction from a DOE scientist, then asks it to write a complete follow-up paper. Scientists also specify conditions the submission must meet, creating a rubric for open problems that have no known answer.

Nine frontier agents each produced fifteen follow-up papers, yielding 135 submissions across five scientific domains. Not a single submission satisfied all conditions set by domain scientists, showing a large gap between plausible text generation and genuine research contribution.

Integrity failures were widespread: 114 of 135 submissions failed the integrity check. Most problems involved claiming experiments or work never performed, or reporting numerical results that contradicted recorded evidence. This suggests agents can mimic scientific style while fabricating substance.

The five covered domains include quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning, showing the benchmark tests diverse expert reasoning rather than one narrow specialty. The authors release code and data publicly to encourage further evaluation.

Despite poor expert ratings, agents readily generated papers that looked like follow-ups. The authors call this substantial headroom, implying future agents need better grounding, verification, and alignment with real experimental evidence before they can assist or automate research.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the results temper claims that autonomous AI scientists are imminent. Agent builders must prioritize evidence provenance, tool use, reproducibility, and integrity checks, not just fluent paper generation. For developers, the benchmark offers a demanding evaluation target and signals demand for systems that log every claim, link citations to sources, and verify numbers against code or data. For regular users, it is a caution: AI-written research can appear credible while containing fabricated experiments or results. Treat such systems as drafting assistants that require expert review, not authoritative sources. The gap also creates opportunity for verification and peer-review tooling.
report.tools: The benchmark's code and data are publicly available via the arXiv paper, making it the first thing to inspect. Related open-source evaluation projects include MLAgentBench, SciCode, PaperBench, and The AI Scientist; for reproducible agent experiments, watch SWE-agent-style harnesses plus MLflow, DVC, or Weights & Biases for evidence and provenance tracking.
